meta.units: Rates in US dollars per 100 cubic feet (HCF, about 748 gallons). Fiscal year runs July 1 - June 30 and is named for the year it ends. Rental payments and debt service in millions of dollars.
meta.primary_sources: NYC Water Board rate schedules, rate reports ("Blue Books"), adoption public notices, minutes, and audited NYC Water and Sewer System financial statements, all at nyc.gov/assets/nycwaterboard.

reasons.reason: Debt service (45% of FY2015 budget) from a capital program driven largely by unfunded state and federal mandates (the Croton filtration plant, ultraviolet treatment for the Catskill and Delaware supplies and the Newtown Creek plant).
reasons.quote: debt service is a direct result of DEP’s massive capital construction projects, which have been largely driven by unfunded mandates

reasons.reason: Debt service is the largest budget component (44%), tied to mandate-driven capital program; operating savings partly offset costs.
reasons.quote: largest component of the System’s annual budget will be its debt service, accounting for 44% of the total revenue needed in FY2016.

reasons.reason: Mayor eliminated the rental payment to the City for FY2017; the 2.1% increase adopted alongside a $183 homeowner credit was later annulled and repealed, so rates did not change.
reasons.quote: In FY 2017, Mayor de Blasio will eliminate the rental payment and not request an estimated payment of $244 million.

reasons.reason: Board repealed the FY2017 2.1% increase in January 2018 after court annulment.

reasons.quote: a one-time credit issued to residential properties holders with three or fewer units totaling $121 million

reasons.reason: Debt service and capital investment are the largest budget driver (58%).

reasons.reason: Capital additions include state- and federally mandated Hillview Reservoir treatment improvements and Delaware Aqueduct repair.
reasons.quote: Hillview Reservoir water treatment improvements

reasons.reason: Growing capital plan and higher vendor and personnel costs; strong collections (enforcement, including the lien sale) held the increase to 3.7%.
reasons.quote: Higher projected capital spending due to the growing size of the agency’s capital investment plan.

reasons.reason: Strong FY2025 collections from enforcement, including the lien sale.
reasons.quote: FY25 to-date represents one of the highest revenue performances in the system’s history, driven by a wide portfolio of enforcement initiatives including the lien sale.

reasons.reason: Higher operating costs for vendors and personnel and capital spending; increase cut from a forecast 7.0% to 6.0% on strong revenues; City rental payment budgeted at $312M.

reasons.reason: Increase reduced from the original 7.0% forecast.
reasons.quote: take a forward-looking approach with a 6.0% proposed rate increase, reduced from the original forecast of a 7.0% increase.

Typical-bill basis changes: 100,000 gal (FY2009-10 report), 80,000 gal (FY2010-FY2019), 70,000 gal (FY2019 onward) for single-family; multifamily unit 85,000 gal in FY2009, then 52,000. No official FY2017 typical bill; no FY2016/FY2017 metered multifamily figure; none before FY2009 found.

Sewer and combined $/HCF are derived (water x 1.59, rounded to the cent). This matches every published wastewater figure checked (FY2009-FY2020 reports). DEP's "How We Bill You" page (nyc.gov/site/dep/pay-my-bills/how-we-bill-you.page) states FY2027 combined is $13.50/HCF, which does not equal $5.35 x 2.59 = $13.86; treat the DEP page figure as unreliable.

Rental payment before FY2006 not collected (older CAFRs not posted on the Board site). FY2010-FY2015 rental payments were partly offset by a "rental rebate" the City returned (recorded as System revenue); rebate amounts not tabulated here.
